opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot. Anthropic moves fast, and there are always far more interesting problems than people to work on them, so being deliberate about where I spend my time matters.

My first filter is usually: what's the biggest gap between what the models *can* do and what people are actually able to get out of them today? A lot of my work has been around agents and coding, and in that space you constantly see a model that's capable of something in principle but trips up in practice. Maybe the tooling is clunky, maybe the scaffolding isn't right, maybe we're just not measuring the right thing. Those gaps are really high-leverage, because closing one can unlock a whole category of use cases.

The second thing is that I try to stay very close to real usage. I'll use the models heavily myself on actual work, not just toy tasks, and I pay attention to where I get frustrated. If I'm annoyed by something, there's a good chance thousands of other people are too. That gut-level frustration is often a better signal than any roadmap document.

Third, and this is more of an Anthropic-specific thing, I think about whether the work compounds. Does it make the next model better? Does it give us better evals, better feedback, a better understanding of how these systems behave? Work that only helps a single product feature is fine, but work that feeds back into research and makes everything downstream better is usually the stuff I get most excited about.

And then the last piece is just being willing to drop things. Ideas that seemed important six months ago can get completely leapfrogged by a new model release. So I try to hold plans loosely, check in on whether something's still the highest-value thing, and not get too attached. In this field, the ability to re-prioritize quickly is almost more important than picking perfectly the first time.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes high-impact work for Anthropic and mentions personal frustration and excitement, but it does not clearly describe balancing personal interests against where Erik can contribute the most value.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I keep coming back to is "what's the thing that nobody is doing that would be really embarrassing if we don't do it?" Anthropic is still small relative to the surface area of problems, and there's a lot of stuff that's obviously important but sits in the gap between teams. My bias is to go stand in that gap.

The way I actually run it in my head is something like: if I imagine the model six months from now, what's the bottleneck on it being useful? Early on that was obviously capabilities, and that's still true in a lot of ways, but increasingly the bottleneck is the stuff around the model. Can it use tools well? Can it work for a long time without going off the rails? Can it tell you when it's unsure instead of confidently making something up? Those feel like the places where a relatively small amount of focused effort moves the needle a lot, and they're also the places where you learn the most about what the model is actually like, which feeds back into everything else.

The other thing I'd say, and this comes from my startup background, is that I try to pick things where I can get a signal fast. I'd rather do the ugly version in a week, see if it works at all, and then decide whether it deserves a real investment, than spend two months on the principled version of something that turns out not to matter. With models this is especially true because your intuitions are often wrong. You think "oh, the model will obviously be able to do X," and it just can't, or you think something will be hard and it falls out for free. So I optimize pretty hard for cheap experiments.

And then there's a boring but real part, which is just taste and what I'm excited about. I like agents, I like the idea of the model doing real work in the world, and it turns out that's also where a lot of the leverage is right now. So I don't fight that too much. If I'm excited about it, I'll push harder, and that compounds.

r001.rationale: He weighs company impact by targeting neglected gaps and bottlenecks where focused work can move the needle, while also factoring in what excites him and where he feels leverage.

astra-6.text: I think about it in terms of leverage: where can I spend my time and make the biggest difference? With AI moving so quickly, that also means asking whether a problem needs engineering work today or whether the next generation of models might make it much easier. I’m drawn to work that gets more useful as the models improve. And then I like to build something small, get feedback, and use that to decide whether it deserves a bigger investment.

sol-6.1.text: I tend to start with a bottleneck: what’s keeping us from making progress, and is there something I can build that would help? I like problems where I can get close to the work, try something quickly, and get feedback. Sometimes that means improving the model, and sometimes it means improving the tools around it. The question is where I can have the most impact, rather than whether the work fits neatly into a particular category.
